H1.text: A bowling ball rolls down a lane. A coin rolls off the table. A ring rolls down a slope.

H2.text: They all start from rest, but they do not all roll at the same speed.

H3.text: Diya lets a ring, a disc and a ball go from the same height on the same slope.

H4.text: Same start, same slope. Yet the ball wins and the ring comes last, every time. Why?

H5.text: The answer is hidden in the energy of rolling.

P1.text: A rolling body does two things at once. It moves forward, and it spins.

P2.text: So it has two kinds of kinetic energy. One half m v squared, for moving forward.

P3.text: And one half I omega squared, for spinning. Its total energy is the sum of the two.

P4.text: Note: rolling is not in the current NCERT book. It is in the JEE Advanced syllabus.

S1.text: Our motion notebook. A thirty degree slope, two metres long, one metre high. A ring, a disc and a ball.

S2.text: Let them go. The ball pulls ahead, then the disc. The ring is last.

S3.text: On the graph, each speed grows in a straight line. The ball's line is the steepest.

S4.text: At the bottom: the ball moves at three point seven four metres per second, the disc at three point six two, and the ring at three point one three.

S5.text: Slow-mo replay. Freeze in the middle of the race.

S6.text: Look at the energy bars. Each body turned the same height into energy, but split it in different ways.

S7.text: The ring puts half of its energy into spinning. The disc puts one third. The ball, only two sevenths.

S8.text: Less energy spent on spinning means more for moving forward. So the ball moves fastest.

S9.text: Now you try. A heavy disc and a light disc, the same size, race down the slope. Which one wins? Pause and decide.

S10.text: It is a tie! Mass cancels out. Only the shape decides the speed.

R1.text: Why does the ring lose? Link by link.

R2.text: All of the ring's mass sits at the rim, far from the axis.

R3.text: Mass far from the axis makes spinning cost more energy.

R4.text: So the ring spends the biggest share on spin, and has the least left for speed.

D1.text: Now the rule, one step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. Total energy is one half m v squared, plus one half I omega squared.

D3.text: Step two. Put omega equal to v over R, and I equal to m k squared. K equals one half m v squared, times one plus k squared over R squared.

D4.text: Step three. The bottom point does not slip, so friction does no work. So m g h equals that energy.

D5.text: Step four. v equals root of two g h, over one plus k squared over R squared. The mass cancels.

D6.text: Step five. For a ring, k squared over R squared is one. For a disc, a half. For a ball, two fifths. The smallest value wins.

T1.text: Remember this. A rolling body shares its energy between moving and spinning. The less it spins, the faster it goes.

K1.text: Side by side. A rolling ball must spin, so part of its energy goes into spin.

K2.text: A block slides down a smooth slope of the same height. It does not spin at all.

K3.text: Now you try. Which reaches the bottom first: the rolling ball, or the sliding block? Pause and decide.

K4.text: The sliding block! None of its energy goes into spin, so all of it becomes speed. Four point four three metres per second.

W2.text: A solid ball of mass two kilograms rolls without slipping at three metres per second. Find its total kinetic energy, and the part that is spin.

W3.text: Moving forward: one half times two times three squared. Nine joules.

W4.text: For a solid ball, k squared over R squared is two fifths. So spin is two fifths of nine. Three point six joules.

W5.text: Total: nine plus three point six. Twelve point six joules.

X2.text: Many students think friction on a rolling body wastes energy, like on a sliding one.

X3.text: In rolling without slipping, the contact point is at rest. So friction does no work. It only moves energy from forward motion into spin.

E1.text: Where is this asked? In races down a slope, energy shares, and how high a rolling body climbs.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A solid cylinder rolls without slipping towards a slope at four metres per second. g is ten. How high up the slope does it climb? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. One point two metres.

A2.text: For a solid cylinder, k squared over R squared is one half.

A3.text: Energy: one half m v squared, times one point five, equals m g h. The mass cancels.

A4.text: So h equals sixteen times one point five, over twenty. One point two metres.

Y2.text: One. Why does the ring come last in the race?

Y3.text: Two. Why do a heavy disc and a light disc of the same size tie?

Y4.text: Three. Why does friction do no work on a body that rolls without slipping?
